extends.description: Config files to start from, relative to this one; later ones and this file win.

include.description: Globs of files to lint, relative to this file. Default: every JS/TS file.

ignore.description: Globs of files or folders to skip, relative to this file.

tier.description: The highest tier --fix applies: exact (same behaviour for every input), typed (for every input the types allow) or assumed (relies on a stated assumption). Default: typed.

obscure.description: Let --fix apply fixes that are correct but hard to read, such as `x | 0`. Default: false.

target.description: The newest ES version fixes may write, for code that runs as written (no compiler in between). A fix that needs newer syntax or a newer built-in is reported without a fix. Default: the tsconfig's target when tsc does not emit, and the lib for built-ins.

minImpact.description: Only report rules with at least this impact. Default: low.

maxSlowdown.description: Skip rules whose fix measured more than this much slower than the original code on some engine, compiler tier or input size the bench covers. Default "10%", to allow for measurement noise; "0%" drops every fix that was slower anywhere; "any" runs them all. Rules without a measured fix always run.

targets.description: Where the code runs. Only the engines of these targets (V8: node, deno, chrome, edge; JavaScriptCore: bun, safari) count against maxSlowdown, so a fix that is slower only on the other engine can run. Unset: every engine.

domains.description: Groups for one library or tool. They join the presets only where a package.json, in the file's folder or above, depends on one of their packages.

typescript.description: auto (default): in the presets when a package.json lists typescript; on: always; off: never. Explicit rule and group settings still apply.

react.description: auto (default): in the presets when a package.json lists react or preact; on: always; off: never. Explicit rule and group settings still apply.

overrides.description: Settings for some files, applied in order after the rest of the config.

tier.description: The highest tier --fix applies: exact (same behaviour for every input), typed (for every input the types allow) or assumed (relies on a stated assumption). Default: typed.

obscure.description: Let --fix apply fixes that are correct but hard to read, such as `x | 0`. Default: false.

target.description: The newest ES version fixes may write, for code that runs as written (no compiler in between). A fix that needs newer syntax or a newer built-in is reported without a fix. Default: the tsconfig's target when tsc does not emit, and the lib for built-ins.

Level.description: off disables the rule; on enables it with its default severity; info, warn and error also set the severity.

tier.description: Treat this rule's fixes as at least this tier (it can only raise them), or none to drop them.

Rules.description: Applied in order: preset, then groups, then single rules.

preset.description: The starting set: recommended (default), all, or none.

accumulate.description: The accumulate group: spread-in-accumulator, accumulate-by-copy-in-loop. A level for all of them, or settings per rule.

spread-in-accumulator.markdownDescription:
`xs.reduce((acc, x) => ({ ...acc, [k]: v }), {})` → mutate `acc`

Spreading the accumulator copies everything collected so far on every step, which makes reduce O(n²). The initial value is a fresh literal, so mutating it is invisible to callers.

high impact. Fixes: typed or assumed.

accumulate-by-copy-in-loop.markdownDescription:
`xs = [...xs, x]` / `xs = xs.concat(x)` / `o = {...o, k: v}` inside a loop

Rebuilding the collection on each iteration copies everything gathered so far: O(n²) time and garbage. Push or assign in place.

high impact. Fixes: assumed.

lookup.description: The lookup group: lookup-in-loop, array-literal-lookup, quadratic-array-mutation. A level for all of them, or settings per rule.

lookup-in-loop.markdownDescription:
Linear search (`includes`/`indexOf`/`find`/`some`) inside a loop

A linear search inside a loop makes the whole thing O(n·m). Build a Set or Map once before the loop and each lookup becomes O(1).

high impact. Report only.

array-literal-lookup.markdownDescription:
`['a', 'b'].includes(x)` inside a function → `x === 'a' || x === 'b'` or a hoisted Set

The array literal is rebuilt on every call and then searched linearly. A few comparisons need no allocation; for longer lists a module-level Set gives O(1) lookups.

medium impact. Fixes: exact.

quadratic-array-mutation.markdownDescription:
`shift`/`unshift`/`splice` inside a loop

These move every following element. Inside a loop over the same data that is O(n²); a head index, a reverse, or a single compaction pass is O(n).

medium impact. Report only.

async.description: The async group: await-in-loop, sequential-await. A level for all of them, or settings per rule.

await-in-loop.markdownDescription:
`await` inside a loop body, or a promise chain built with `reduce`

Each iteration waits for the previous one, so total time is the sum of all latencies. If iterations are independent, start them all and `await Promise.all(...)` (or batch them to bound concurrency). Loops that poll, retry, pace themselves, stop early, carry a value to the next iteration, or drive one browser page, editor or terminal are left alone.

high impact. Report only.

sequential-await.markdownDescription:
Back-to-back independent `await`s → `Promise.all`

`const a = await f(); const b = await g();` waits for f before starting g, even though g never reads `a`. Promise.all overlaps them. (Unsafe: g now starts before f settles, and a rejection in f no longer prevents g from running.)

high impact. Fixes: assumed.

arrays.description: The arrays group: filter-first, filter-length-to-some, map-flat-to-flatmap, unused-map, redundant-array-copy, chained-array-methods, sort-for-extremum, math-minmax-spread, typed-array-subarray, typed-array-round-trip. A level for all of them, or settings per rule.

filter-first.markdownDescription:
`xs.filter(f)[0]` → `xs.find(f)`

filter visits every element and allocates a new array; find stops at the first match and allocates nothing.

medium impact. Fixes: typed or assumed.

filter-length-to-some.markdownDescription:
`xs.filter(f).length > 0` → `xs.some(f)`

Counting matches allocates an array and visits every element; some() short-circuits on the first match.

medium impact. Fixes: typed or assumed.

map-flat-to-flatmap.markdownDescription:
`xs.map(f).flat()` → `xs.flatMap(f)`

flatMap does one pass and skips the intermediate array.

low impact. Fixes: typed or assumed.

unused-map.markdownDescription:
`xs.map(f);` with the result ignored → `xs.forEach(f)`

map allocates and fills a result array that nobody reads.

medium impact. Fixes: typed or assumed.

redundant-array-copy.markdownDescription:
`[...xs].map(f)` → `xs.map(f)` for non-mutating methods

Copying an array before a method that does not mutate it costs an O(n) allocation for nothing.

medium impact. Fixes: typed or assumed.

chained-array-methods.markdownDescription:
`xs.filter(f).map(g)` chains allocate an array per step

Each map/filter step allocates a full intermediate array and walks it again. One loop (or one reduce) does it in a single pass.

medium impact. Report only.

sort-for-extremum.markdownDescription:
`xs.sort()[0]` to find a min/max

Sorting is O(n log n) (and sort() mutates); finding the min or max is a single O(n) pass.

medium impact. Report only.

math-minmax-spread.markdownDescription:
`Math.max(...xs)` on large arrays

Spreading pushes every element onto the stack: slow for big arrays and a RangeError past ~100k elements. A loop is faster and safe.

medium impact. Report only.

typed-array-subarray.markdownDescription:
`ta.slice(a, b)` on a typed array → `ta.subarray(a, b)`

On a typed array, `slice` allocates a new buffer and copies the elements; `subarray` makes a view over the same memory in constant time. The view shares memory, so it is `typed` only when the result is read right away (`indexOf`, `TextDecoder.decode`, a spread into `Math.max`); otherwise writes to either array would show in the other.

medium impact. Fixes: typed or assumed.

typed-array-round-trip.markdownDescription:
`new Uint8Array(Array.from(ta))` or `new Uint8Array([...ta])` → `new Uint8Array(ta)`

The plain array in the middle boxes every element and is thrown away. A typed array constructor copies another typed array directly, converting each element the same way.

medium impact. Fixes: typed.

loops.description: The loops group: foreach-to-for, for-of-to-indexed, for-in-array, cache-array-length. A level for all of them, or settings per rule.

foreach-to-for.markdownDescription:
`xs.forEach(x => ...)` → indexed `for` loop

An indexed loop has no per-element function call, so nothing has to be inlined. It is fastest in every engine tier, especially for large or polymorphic arrays. Holes in sparse arrays are skipped, as forEach does.

medium impact. Fixes: typed or assumed.

for-of-to-indexed.markdownDescription:
`for (const x of xs)` → indexed `for` loop (proven arrays only)

for-of runs the iterator protocol. Optimizing compilers can remove that cost, but baseline tiers and cold code still pay it on every step, and an indexed loop never does.

low impact. Fixes: typed. Not in the recommended preset.

for-in-array.markdownDescription:
`for (const k in array)` → indexed loop

for-in enumerates string keys, including inherited ones, through a slow generic path. Indices come back as strings, so every `xs[k]` also converts the key. Note: the fix makes the index a number.

high impact. Fixes: assumed.

cache-array-length.markdownDescription:
`for (let i = 0; i < xs.length; i++)` → cache `xs.length`

Measured, it makes no difference once a loop is optimized: TurboFan, FTL and DFG already keep the length in a register (1.00–1.01x). It helps only in the interpreter and baseline tiers (about 1.2x on Sparkplug and LLInt), i.e. code that never gets hot. Off by default for that reason (`bench/FINDINGS.md`).

low impact. Fixes: typed or assumed. Not in the recommended preset.

strings.description: The strings group: split-join-to-replaceall, regex-to-string-method, match-to-test, indexof-to-startswith, regexp-constructor-literal, catastrophic-regex, string-flatten-in-loop, regexp-in-loop. A level for all of them, or settings per rule.

split-join-to-replaceall.markdownDescription:
`s.split(a).join(b)` → `s.replaceAll(a, b)`

split/join allocates an array of every piece and then concatenates them again. replaceAll does a single pass. (Needs ES2021.)

medium impact. Fixes: typed or assumed.

regex-to-string-method.markdownDescription:
`/^abc/.test(s)` → `s.startsWith('abc')` (also endsWith, includes, ===)

Plain-text patterns don't need the regex engine. String methods skip regex compilation and matcher setup and are usually several times faster.

medium impact. Fixes: typed or assumed.

match-to-test.markdownDescription:
`s.match(re)` / `re.exec(s)` used as a boolean → `re.test(s)`

match and exec allocate a result array with captures; test only returns a boolean.

medium impact. Fixes: typed or assumed.

indexof-to-startswith.markdownDescription:
`s.indexOf(x) === 0` → `s.startsWith(x)`

When the prefix is missing, indexOf keeps scanning the whole string. startsWith compares only the prefix.

medium impact. Fixes: typed or assumed.

regexp-constructor-literal.markdownDescription:
`new RegExp('a+b', 'g')` with constant arguments → `/a+b/g`

A regex literal is parsed once and its compiled code is reused by the engine at that site. A constant RegExp constructor inside a function re-parses its source and looks up the cache on every call.

low impact. Fixes: exact.

catastrophic-regex.markdownDescription:
Nested quantifiers like `(a+)+` or `(\w+\s?)*`

A repeated group whose body can match the same text several ways backtracks exponentially when the match fails (ReDoS). Make the inner part unambiguous, or use a possessive-style rewrite.

high impact. Report only.

string-flatten-in-loop.markdownDescription:
A string grown with `+=` and searched or indexed in the same loop

`s += x` builds a rope, which is cheap. A read such as `s.charCodeAt(i)`, `s[i]` or `s.indexOf(x)` flattens the rope into one buffer, copying the whole string. Doing both in each iteration copies the string every time: O(n²). Keep what you need to read in a separate variable, or collect parts in an array and `join` once.

high impact. Report only.

regexp-in-loop.markdownDescription:
`new RegExp(x)` with the same `x` on every iteration of a loop

The pattern does not change between iterations, but each `new RegExp` allocates an object and looks the pattern up in the engine's regexp cache. Build it once before the loop. A hoisted regexp with the `g` or `y` flag keeps `lastIndex` between uses, so reset it or use `String.prototype.match`/`replace`, which do.

low impact. Report only.

objects.description: The objects group: object-assign-to-spread, object-entries-iteration, delete-property, object-keys-emptiness, large-object-literal, object-keys-in-loop, late-property, prototype-mutation. A level for all of them, or settings per rule.

object-assign-to-spread.markdownDescription:
`Object.assign({}, a, b)` → `{ ...a, ...b }`

Object spread into a fresh literal uses the engine's clone fast path (CloneObjectIC in V8). Object.assign goes through the generic [[Set]] path, one property at a time.

medium impact. Fixes: typed.

object-entries-iteration.markdownDescription:
`for (const [k] / [, v] of Object.entries(o))` → `Object.keys` / `Object.values`

Object.entries allocates a [key, value] array per property. A loop that uses only the keys or only the values gets them from Object.keys or Object.values without the pairs.

medium impact. Fixes: exact.

delete-property.markdownDescription:
`delete obj.prop`

On V8, deleting a property drops the object from fast hidden-class mode into slow dictionary mode for good: reads measured 1.6–18x slower than after assigning undefined. JavaScriptCore keeps such objects fast. For a dictionary with many keys (hundreds or more), a Map is faster; with a few dozen, the object is. On arrays, delete leaves a hole.

medium impact. Report only.

object-keys-emptiness.markdownDescription:
`Object.keys(o).length === 0` to test for an empty object

This builds an array of every key just to see whether there is at least one. A `for (const k in o) { if (Object.hasOwn(o, k)) return false }` helper stops at the first key and allocates nothing.

medium impact. Report only.

large-object-literal.markdownDescription:
Large constant object/array literal → `JSON.parse('...')`

For big constant data (over ~10 kB), the JSON parser is much faster than the JavaScript parser and compiler, which have to handle a far richer grammar (see V8's "cost of JavaScript" guidance). The fix loses the static type in TypeScript, so it is only applied automatically in JS files.

medium impact. Fixes: typed or assumed (obscure). Not in the recommended preset.

object-keys-in-loop.markdownDescription:
`Object.keys(o)` (or values/entries) of an unchanged object inside a loop

Each call allocates a fresh array of every key (and, for entries, a pair per key). When the loop never changes the object, the result is the same every time: compute it once before the loop. In a loop condition (`i < Object.keys(o).length`) it is rebuilt on every iteration.

medium impact. Report only.

late-property.markdownDescription:
`this.x = ...` in a method for a field the class never declares or sets in its constructor

Engines give objects a shape (hidden class, Structure) from the properties they get at construction. Adding one later moves every instance to a new shape and can grow its property storage, and code that sees instances from before and after becomes polymorphic. Declare the field, or set it in the constructor (`this.x = undefined`).

low impact. Report only.

prototype-mutation.markdownDescription:
`Object.setPrototypeOf`, `Reflect.setPrototypeOf` or `__proto__ =` on an existing object

Changing an object's prototype after it exists invalidates the engine's assumptions about it and about code that has seen it; V8 and JSC both deoptimize, and the object may stay slow. Create it with the right prototype: `Object.create(proto)`, a class, or `{ __proto__: proto, ... }` in a literal.

medium impact. Report only.

typescript.description: The typescript group: downlevel-async, define-class-fields, downlevel-private-fields. A level for all of them, or settings per rule.

downlevel-async.markdownDescription:
`async` compiled to generators by a `target` below ES2017

Below ES2017, TypeScript turns each async function into a generator driven by its `__awaiter` helper (async generators and `for await` need ES2018). Calls and awaits measured 2–14x slower than native async on V8 and JSC, at every tier. Every engine since 2017 runs native async, so raise `target` unless you ship to older ones.

medium impact. Report only.

define-class-fields.markdownDescription:
Class fields emitted as `Object.defineProperty` (`useDefineForClassFields` below ES2022)

With `useDefineForClassFields: true` and a `target` below ES2022, TypeScript writes every instance field as an `Object.defineProperty` call in the constructor. Constructing such objects measured 4–100x slower than native fields or plain assignment, on V8 and JSC. Set `target` to ES2022 or later (native fields keep the same semantics), or drop the option if nothing relies on define semantics.

high impact. Report only.

downlevel-private-fields.markdownDescription:
`#private` members compiled to WeakMaps by a `target` below ES2022

Below ES2022, TypeScript emulates `#private` fields and methods with a WeakMap or WeakSet per member and a checking helper on every access. Construction and access measured 5x to over 200x slower than native private fields, on V8 and JSC. Raise `target` to ES2022, or use TypeScript's `private` keyword, which emits a plain property.

high impact. Report only.

react.description: The react group: inline-prop-to-memo, inline-context-value, unstable-key. A level for all of them, or settings per rule.

inline-prop-to-memo.markdownDescription:
A `memo` or `PureComponent` component given an object, array, function or element made during render

`memo` and `PureComponent` skip a render only when every prop is the same as last time (`Object.is`). An inline `{}`, `[]`, arrow or JSX element is a new value on every render, so the component re-renders every time and also pays for the comparison. Hoist constants out of the component, and wrap the rest in `useMemo` or `useCallback`. With React Compiler, this is done for you.

medium impact. Report only.

inline-context-value.markdownDescription:
A context provider whose `value` is an object, array or function made during render

Every component that reads a context re-renders when its `value` changes (`Object.is`), however deep it is and even inside `memo`. A `value={{ user, setUser }}` built in render is new each time, so every consumer re-renders whenever the provider does. Wrap the value in `useMemo` (and its functions in `useCallback`), or hoist it. With React Compiler, this is done for you.

medium impact. Report only.

unstable-key.markdownDescription:
A JSX `key` from `Math.random()`, `crypto.randomUUID()`, `Date.now()` or a fresh id

React matches elements across renders by `key`. A key that changes on every render makes React unmount the old element and mount a new one each time: its whole subtree is rebuilt, its DOM replaced, and its state and effects reset. Key by a stable id from the data, or generate ids once, when the data is created.

high impact. Report only.

misc.description: The misc group: date-now, math-pow-to-mul, bitwise-trunc, dynamic-code, dom-in-loop, arguments-object, postmessage-transfer, passive-listener, scroll-layout-read, gpu-sync-in-frame, per-frame-allocation. A level for all of them, or settings per rule.

date-now.markdownDescription:
`new Date().getTime()` / `+new Date()` → `Date.now()`

Date.now() returns the timestamp without allocating a Date object.

low impact. Fixes: exact.

math-pow-to-mul.markdownDescription:
`Math.pow(x, 2)` / `x ** 2` → `x * x`

Squaring with a multiply is one instruction, while pow goes through the generic power routine (or a builtin call in lower tiers). The results are bit-identical for numbers.

low impact. Fixes: typed or assumed.

bitwise-trunc.markdownDescription:
`Math.trunc(x)` / `Math.floor(x)` → `x | 0` (int32 only)

`x | 0` truncates to a 32-bit integer in one instruction and tells the JIT the value is a small integer, which keeps the arithmetic after it in int32. It is wrong outside ±2³¹ and for negative values with floor, so the fix is unsafe: only use it where you know the range.

low impact. Fixes: assumed (obscure). Not in the recommended preset.

dynamic-code.markdownDescription:
`eval`, `new Function`, and `with`

Direct eval and `with` make every variable in the enclosing scopes dynamically resolvable, which blocks inlining and register allocation for those functions. new Function re-parses and compiles its source on every call.

high impact. Report only.

dom-in-loop.markdownDescription:
DOM queries and layout reads inside loops

Querying the DOM walks the tree. Layout reads such as offsetHeight or getBoundingClientRect force a synchronous reflow when styles are dirty, and interleaving them with writes in a loop causes layout thrashing. Query once and batch reads before writes.

high impact. Report only.

arguments-object.markdownDescription:
`arguments` that escapes, or is written → rest parameters

Optimizing compilers never allocate `arguments` when the function only reads `arguments.length` or `arguments[i]`, or passes it to `f.apply(this, arguments)`. Passing it anywhere else, storing it, or writing to it forces a real object (in sloppy mode one that aliases the parameters). Rest parameters give a real array and are always cheap.

low impact. Report only.

postmessage-transfer.markdownDescription:
`postMessage(buffer)` of an ArrayBuffer or typed array without a transfer list

Without a transfer list, `postMessage` copies the whole buffer (structured clone). Transferring moves it in constant time: `postMessage(ta, [ta.buffer])` for a worker or port, `postMessage(ta, origin, [ta.buffer])` for a window. The sender's buffer is then detached, so only do it when the sender is done with it.

medium impact. Report only.

passive-listener.markdownDescription:
`wheel`/`touchstart`/`touchmove` listener that never calls `preventDefault`, without `{ passive: true }`

The browser cannot scroll until a non-passive wheel or touch listener returns, because it might call `preventDefault`. A listener that never does can say so with `{ passive: true }`, and scrolling no longer waits for it.

medium impact. Fixes: typed or assumed.

scroll-layout-read.markdownDescription:
A `scroll` or `resize` listener that reads layout

Scroll and resize fire many times per frame, and each layout read (`getBoundingClientRect`, `offsetTop`) can force a synchronous reflow. `IntersectionObserver` answers visibility questions and `ResizeObserver` size ones without polling; otherwise read once per frame inside `requestAnimationFrame`.

medium impact. Report only.

gpu-sync-in-frame.markdownDescription:
`gl.getError()`, `getParameter`, `readPixels` and other GPU round trips inside a frame callback

WebGL calls are queued for the GPU. A query such as `getError` or `readPixels` makes the CPU wait until the queue drains, every frame, which stalls the pipeline. Check errors only in debug builds, cache parameters at start-up, and read pixels asynchronously (a pixel buffer and `fenceSync` in WebGL2).

high impact. Report only.

per-frame-allocation.markdownDescription:
WebGL objects, canvas contexts or typed arrays created inside a frame callback

Creating GPU buffers and textures, looking up a canvas context, or allocating typed arrays on every frame churns GPU memory and the garbage collector, which shows up as dropped frames. Create them once and reuse them (`bufferSubData`, `texSubImage2D`, a scratch typed array).

medium impact. Report only.

medium impact. Fixes: typed.

foreach-to-for.markdownDescription:
`xs.forEach(x => ...)` → indexed `for` loop

An indexed loop has no per-element function call, so nothing has to be inlined. It is fastest in every engine tier, especially for large or polymorphic arrays. Holes in sparse arrays are skipped, as forEach does.

medium impact. Fixes: typed or assumed.

for-of-to-indexed.markdownDescription:
`for (const x of xs)` → indexed `for` loop (proven arrays only)

for-of runs the iterator protocol. Optimizing compilers can remove that cost, but baseline tiers and cold code still pay it on every step, and an indexed loop never does.

low impact. Fixes: typed. Not in the recommended preset.

for-in-array.markdownDescription:
`for (const k in array)` → indexed loop

for-in enumerates string keys, including inherited ones, through a slow generic path. Indices come back as strings, so every `xs[k]` also converts the key. Note: the fix makes the index a number.

high impact. Fixes: assumed.

cache-array-length.markdownDescription:
`for (let i = 0; i < xs.length; i++)` → cache `xs.length`

Measured, it makes no difference once a loop is optimized: TurboFan, FTL and DFG already keep the length in a register (1.00–1.01x). It helps only in the interpreter and baseline tiers (about 1.2x on Sparkplug and LLInt), i.e. code that never gets hot. Off by default for that reason (`bench/FINDINGS.md`).

low impact. Fixes: typed or assumed. Not in the recommended preset.

split-join-to-replaceall.markdownDescription:
`s.split(a).join(b)` → `s.replaceAll(a, b)`

split/join allocates an array of every piece and then concatenates them again. replaceAll does a single pass. (Needs ES2021.)

medium impact. Fixes: typed or assumed.

regex-to-string-method.markdownDescription:
`/^abc/.test(s)` → `s.startsWith('abc')` (also endsWith, includes, ===)

Plain-text patterns don't need the regex engine. String methods skip regex compilation and matcher setup and are usually several times faster.

medium impact. Fixes: typed or assumed.

match-to-test.markdownDescription:
`s.match(re)` / `re.exec(s)` used as a boolean → `re.test(s)`

match and exec allocate a result array with captures; test only returns a boolean.

medium impact. Fixes: typed or assumed.

indexof-to-startswith.markdownDescription:
`s.indexOf(x) === 0` → `s.startsWith(x)`

When the prefix is missing, indexOf keeps scanning the whole string. startsWith compares only the prefix.

medium impact. Fixes: typed or assumed.

regexp-constructor-literal.markdownDescription:
`new RegExp('a+b', 'g')` with constant arguments → `/a+b/g`

A regex literal is parsed once and its compiled code is reused by the engine at that site. A constant RegExp constructor inside a function re-parses its source and looks up the cache on every call.

low impact. Fixes: exact.

catastrophic-regex.markdownDescription:
Nested quantifiers like `(a+)+` or `(\w+\s?)*`

A repeated group whose body can match the same text several ways backtracks exponentially when the match fails (ReDoS). Make the inner part unambiguous, or use a possessive-style rewrite.

high impact. Report only.

string-flatten-in-loop.markdownDescription:
A string grown with `+=` and searched or indexed in the same loop

`s += x` builds a rope, which is cheap. A read such as `s.charCodeAt(i)`, `s[i]` or `s.indexOf(x)` flattens the rope into one buffer, copying the whole string. Doing both in each iteration copies the string every time: O(n²). Keep what you need to read in a separate variable, or collect parts in an array and `join` once.

high impact. Report only.

regexp-in-loop.markdownDescription:
`new RegExp(x)` with the same `x` on every iteration of a loop

The pattern does not change between iterations, but each `new RegExp` allocates an object and looks the pattern up in the engine's regexp cache. Build it once before the loop. A hoisted regexp with the `g` or `y` flag keeps `lastIndex` between uses, so reset it or use `String.prototype.match`/`replace`, which do.

low impact. Report only.

object-assign-to-spread.markdownDescription:
`Object.assign({}, a, b)` → `{ ...a, ...b }`

Object spread into a fresh literal uses the engine's clone fast path (CloneObjectIC in V8). Object.assign goes through the generic [[Set]] path, one property at a time.

medium impact. Fixes: typed.

object-entries-iteration.markdownDescription:
`for (const [k] / [, v] of Object.entries(o))` → `Object.keys` / `Object.values`

Object.entries allocates a [key, value] array per property. A loop that uses only the keys or only the values gets them from Object.keys or Object.values without the pairs.

medium impact. Fixes: exact.

delete-property.markdownDescription:
`delete obj.prop`

On V8, deleting a property drops the object from fast hidden-class mode into slow dictionary mode for good: reads measured 1.6–18x slower than after assigning undefined. JavaScriptCore keeps such objects fast. For a dictionary with many keys (hundreds or more), a Map is faster; with a few dozen, the object is. On arrays, delete leaves a hole.

medium impact. Report only.

object-keys-emptiness.markdownDescription:
`Object.keys(o).length === 0` to test for an empty object

This builds an array of every key just to see whether there is at least one. A `for (const k in o) { if (Object.hasOwn(o, k)) return false }` helper stops at the first key and allocates nothing.

medium impact. Report only.

large-object-literal.markdownDescription:
Large constant object/array literal → `JSON.parse('...')`

For big constant data (over ~10 kB), the JSON parser is much faster than the JavaScript parser and compiler, which have to handle a far richer grammar (see V8's "cost of JavaScript" guidance). The fix loses the static type in TypeScript, so it is only applied automatically in JS files.

medium impact. Fixes: typed or assumed (obscure). Not in the recommended preset.

object-keys-in-loop.markdownDescription:
`Object.keys(o)` (or values/entries) of an unchanged object inside a loop

Each call allocates a fresh array of every key (and, for entries, a pair per key). When the loop never changes the object, the result is the same every time: compute it once before the loop. In a loop condition (`i < Object.keys(o).length`) it is rebuilt on every iteration.

medium impact. Report only.

late-property.markdownDescription:
`this.x = ...` in a method for a field the class never declares or sets in its constructor

Engines give objects a shape (hidden class, Structure) from the properties they get at construction. Adding one later moves every instance to a new shape and can grow its property storage, and code that sees instances from before and after becomes polymorphic. Declare the field, or set it in the constructor (`this.x = undefined`).

low impact. Report only.

prototype-mutation.markdownDescription:
`Object.setPrototypeOf`, `Reflect.setPrototypeOf` or `__proto__ =` on an existing object

Changing an object's prototype after it exists invalidates the engine's assumptions about it and about code that has seen it; V8 and JSC both deoptimize, and the object may stay slow. Create it with the right prototype: `Object.create(proto)`, a class, or `{ __proto__: proto, ... }` in a literal.

medium impact. Report only.

downlevel-async.markdownDescription:
`async` compiled to generators by a `target` below ES2017

Below ES2017, TypeScript turns each async function into a generator driven by its `__awaiter` helper (async generators and `for await` need ES2018). Calls and awaits measured 2–14x slower than native async on V8 and JSC, at every tier. Every engine since 2017 runs native async, so raise `target` unless you ship to older ones.

medium impact. Report only.

define-class-fields.markdownDescription:
Class fields emitted as `Object.defineProperty` (`useDefineForClassFields` below ES2022)

With `useDefineForClassFields: true` and a `target` below ES2022, TypeScript writes every instance field as an `Object.defineProperty` call in the constructor. Constructing such objects measured 4–100x slower than native fields or plain assignment, on V8 and JSC. Set `target` to ES2022 or later (native fields keep the same semantics), or drop the option if nothing relies on define semantics.

high impact. Report only.

downlevel-private-fields.markdownDescription:
`#private` members compiled to WeakMaps by a `target` below ES2022

Below ES2022, TypeScript emulates `#private` fields and methods with a WeakMap or WeakSet per member and a checking helper on every access. Construction and access measured 5x to over 200x slower than native private fields, on V8 and JSC. Raise `target` to ES2022, or use TypeScript's `private` keyword, which emits a plain property.

high impact. Report only.

inline-prop-to-memo.markdownDescription:
A `memo` or `PureComponent` component given an object, array, function or element made during render

`memo` and `PureComponent` skip a render only when every prop is the same as last time (`Object.is`). An inline `{}`, `[]`, arrow or JSX element is a new value on every render, so the component re-renders every time and also pays for the comparison. Hoist constants out of the component, and wrap the rest in `useMemo` or `useCallback`. With React Compiler, this is done for you.

medium impact. Report only.

inline-context-value.markdownDescription:
A context provider whose `value` is an object, array or function made during render

Every component that reads a context re-renders when its `value` changes (`Object.is`), however deep it is and even inside `memo`. A `value={{ user, setUser }}` built in render is new each time, so every consumer re-renders whenever the provider does. Wrap the value in `useMemo` (and its functions in `useCallback`), or hoist it. With React Compiler, this is done for you.

medium impact. Report only.

unstable-key.markdownDescription:
A JSX `key` from `Math.random()`, `crypto.randomUUID()`, `Date.now()` or a fresh id

React matches elements across renders by `key`. A key that changes on every render makes React unmount the old element and mount a new one each time: its whole subtree is rebuilt, its DOM replaced, and its state and effects reset. Key by a stable id from the data, or generate ids once, when the data is created.

high impact. Report only.

date-now.markdownDescription:
`new Date().getTime()` / `+new Date()` → `Date.now()`

Date.now() returns the timestamp without allocating a Date object.

low impact. Fixes: exact.

math-pow-to-mul.markdownDescription:
`Math.pow(x, 2)` / `x ** 2` → `x * x`

Squaring with a multiply is one instruction, while pow goes through the generic power routine (or a builtin call in lower tiers). The results are bit-identical for numbers.

low impact. Fixes: typed or assumed.

bitwise-trunc.markdownDescription:
`Math.trunc(x)` / `Math.floor(x)` → `x | 0` (int32 only)

`x | 0` truncates to a 32-bit integer in one instruction and tells the JIT the value is a small integer, which keeps the arithmetic after it in int32. It is wrong outside ±2³¹ and for negative values with floor, so the fix is unsafe: only use it where you know the range.

low impact. Fixes: assumed (obscure). Not in the recommended preset.

dynamic-code.markdownDescription:
`eval`, `new Function`, and `with`

Direct eval and `with` make every variable in the enclosing scopes dynamically resolvable, which blocks inlining and register allocation for those functions. new Function re-parses and compiles its source on every call.

high impact. Report only.

dom-in-loop.markdownDescription:
DOM queries and layout reads inside loops

Querying the DOM walks the tree. Layout reads such as offsetHeight or getBoundingClientRect force a synchronous reflow when styles are dirty, and interleaving them with writes in a loop causes layout thrashing. Query once and batch reads before writes.

high impact. Report only.

arguments-object.markdownDescription:
`arguments` that escapes, or is written → rest parameters

Optimizing compilers never allocate `arguments` when the function only reads `arguments.length` or `arguments[i]`, or passes it to `f.apply(this, arguments)`. Passing it anywhere else, storing it, or writing to it forces a real object (in sloppy mode one that aliases the parameters). Rest parameters give a real array and are always cheap.

low impact. Report only.

postmessage-transfer.markdownDescription:
`postMessage(buffer)` of an ArrayBuffer or typed array without a transfer list

Without a transfer list, `postMessage` copies the whole buffer (structured clone). Transferring moves it in constant time: `postMessage(ta, [ta.buffer])` for a worker or port, `postMessage(ta, origin, [ta.buffer])` for a window. The sender's buffer is then detached, so only do it when the sender is done with it.

medium impact. Report only.

passive-listener.markdownDescription:
`wheel`/`touchstart`/`touchmove` listener that never calls `preventDefault`, without `{ passive: true }`

The browser cannot scroll until a non-passive wheel or touch listener returns, because it might call `preventDefault`. A listener that never does can say so with `{ passive: true }`, and scrolling no longer waits for it.

medium impact. Fixes: typed or assumed.

scroll-layout-read.markdownDescription:
A `scroll` or `resize` listener that reads layout

Scroll and resize fire many times per frame, and each layout read (`getBoundingClientRect`, `offsetTop`) can force a synchronous reflow. `IntersectionObserver` answers visibility questions and `ResizeObserver` size ones without polling; otherwise read once per frame inside `requestAnimationFrame`.

medium impact. Report only.

gpu-sync-in-frame.markdownDescription:
`gl.getError()`, `getParameter`, `readPixels` and other GPU round trips inside a frame callback

WebGL calls are queued for the GPU. A query such as `getError` or `readPixels` makes the CPU wait until the queue drains, every frame, which stalls the pipeline. Check errors only in debug builds, cache parameters at start-up, and read pixels asynchronously (a pixel buffer and `fenceSync` in WebGL2).

high impact. Report only.

per-frame-allocation.markdownDescription:
WebGL objects, canvas contexts or typed arrays created inside a frame callback

Creating GPU buffers and textures, looking up a canvas context, or allocating typed arrays on every frame churns GPU memory and the garbage collector, which shows up as dropped frames. Create them once and reuse them (`bufferSubData`, `texSubImage2D`, a scratch typed array).

medium impact. Report only.
